results.relation_rationale: No unique exact scalar Result is established for the requested state-and-trait family, and no primary is designated. The paper reports separate state (Table 3) and trait (Table 4) analyses at baseline and luteal phase. Provisional component for explicit scope approval: Table 3 luteal-phase state anxiety scores, estimated mean (SEM) 44.2 (2.4) restricted versus 39.7 (2.1) normal. This is a component of the requested outcome family and occasion set; it is also limited to compliant cycle completers. The broader requested target is retained explicitly, not equated to this component. State baseline means are 38.9 (2.3) versus 36.2 (2.0); state pG=0.13 tests the between-group effect across occasions and pTG=0.48 tests time-by-group interaction, neither a luteal-only p value. Equally eligible competing trait component: baseline 35.3 (2.0) versus 33.2 (1.8), luteal 38.1 (2.2) versus 34.9 (2.0), pG=0.25 and pTG=0.46. There is no source-grounded basis to designate either outcome or occasion primary, and this provisional choice requires explicit host scope approval. The native card cannot combine repeated per-arm values into one joint family card; no joint estimate is invented. The ANOVA includes infertility, cycle number and postrandomization conception; p values are not effect estimates or evidence of equivalence.

reported.analysis_population: 69 cycle completers with adequate compliance to assigned diet: 36 sodium restricted and 33 normal, from 119 randomized (57 restricted, 62 normal). 50 excluded from analysis, mainly cycle cancellations, also diet noncompliance or unknown compliance. Repeated-measurement ANOVA includes diet, primary/secondary infertility, first/repeat cycle and conception/no conception; least-squares subclass means. Not an all-randomized analysis.

results.requested_outcome: State and trait anxiety (Spielberger STAI) during an IVF-ET procedure with vs without dietary sodium restriction (no primary is designated)

comparison_groups.assignment: Dietary sodium restriction, advised intake ≤20 mmol sodium/day, from randomization until pregnancy test or menstruation
Normal sodium diet, ad libitum sodium intake

target.intended_analysis_population: All randomized participants in the comparison groups
target.intended_effect_measure: Assignment effect of sodium restriction versus normal intake on STAI state and trait anxiety; provisional reported component is luteal-phase state-anxiety group means from the repeated-measurement model, not a reported difference estimate.

measurement.method: Spielberger STAI state and trait anxiety, separately scored from 20 to 80; neither is designated primary.
measurement.metric: State and trait anxiety (Spielberger STAI) during an IVF-ET procedure with vs without dietary sodium restriction (no primary is designated)

target.outcome_definition: State and trait anxiety (Spielberger STAI) during an IVF-ET procedure with vs without dietary sodium restriction (no primary is designated)

time_point_or_window.description: During the IVF-ET procedure: baseline immediately before randomization (about 10 days before ovarian stimulation) and luteal phase 12 days after ovum pick-up, before pregnancy-test knowledge. Provisional reported component: luteal-phase state anxiety estimated means from the two-occasion model.

counterevidence.implication: Patients were not informed about the possible role of sodium restriction on coping skills; this conceals the hypothesis, not their assigned intervention.

answers.justification: Women implemented either an advised sodium-restricted diet or normal ad libitum intake following dietician instructions. They therefore knew the diet they were assigned during the period producing the luteal state-anxiety scores. Concealing the coping hypothesis does not conceal the actual diet.

Professional dieticians delivered instructions for sodium restriction versus normal intake and compliance was assessed against assigned diet. Intervention-delivery personnel probably knew allocation. The report does not establish blinding of all other IVF staff.
unknowns: Awareness of other IVF carers is not described.

answers.justification: Table 1 reports six women with no diet compliance and four with unknown compliance, while follicle-based cancellations were protocol-defined. These facts establish adherence issues and planned clinical stopping criteria, but do not say whether nonadherence or additional care arose from recruitment, disappointment with allocation, or trial-personnel behaviour. Awareness alone is not proof of a trial-context deviation, and its absence is also not established.
unknowns: Causes of nonadherence and any non-protocol co-interventions attributable to the trial context.

bases.stopping_rationale: Diet/Randomization/Psychological tests methods, Table 1 and Discussion were inspected in the sole captured article. They specify compliance criteria and cancellations but not causes of adherence departures; no protocol or additional conduct Source is captured.
bases.unresolved_premise: Trial-context causation of deviations remains unknown.

counterevidence.implication: Authors claim similar possible selection bias across diet groups; this does not establish that a compliant-completer analysis estimates the randomized assignment effect.

answers.justification: The diet analysis explicitly retains only cycle completers with adequate assigned-diet compliance. Ten exclusions are attributed to no or unknown diet compliance (restricted 6, normal 4), so this is an adherence-restricted analysis rather than an assignment analysis merely excluding missing outcomes. The other cycle-related unavailable outcomes are considered separately in D3. Retained women remain labelled by assignment, but compliance selection is inappropriate for the assignment effect. Including conception as a postrandomization model factor is an additional unresolved estimand concern, not a correction for selection.
unknowns: Whether any compliance-excluded women had measured luteal STAI and the detailed model parameterization.

counterevidence.implication: Noncompliance counts are small compared with cycle-related dropouts and present in both arms. The authors' similar-selection claim is reassuring context but does not rule out substantial impact of adherence-based selection on the assignment contrast.

Noncompliance counts are small compared with cycle-related dropouts and present in both arms. The authors' similar-selection claim is reassuring context but does not rule out substantial impact of adherence-based selection on the assignment contrast.

answers.justification: There is probable potential for substantial impact from selecting on postassignment diet compliance: ten women were excluded for absent/unknown compliance, six of 57 restricted and four of 62 normal. This is a material portion of the randomized sample for a continuous anxiety outcome, and adherence to a burdensome dietary intervention may select women by coping-related characteristics relevant to anxiety. A compliant-completer model does not adjust for this selection. This is a judgment about potential, not proof of bias, and does not count all 50 exclusions as observed-outcome adherence exclusions; most cycle-related absent measurements belong to D3.
unknowns: Actual STAI values and prognostic characteristics of the compliance-excluded women, overlap with missing measurements, and magnitude/direction of bias.

bases.stopping_rationale: Table 1, compliant-completer population description and repeated-measurement methods contain the analysis exclusions but no all-randomized or adherence-adjusted estimate; the captured inventory offers no additional analysis Source.
bases.unresolved_premise: Magnitude and direction of adherence-selection bias cannot be quantified.

answers.justification: The selected state-anxiety component is measured with the Spielberger STAI state scale, explicitly intended to assess anxiety at a given moment, with 20 items and a 20-80 score range. This is a suitable established construct measure for the luteal occasion; no poor validity or inability to detect plausible differences is reported. This does not establish trial-specific psychometric performance.
unknowns: Trial-specific reliability, item completeness and scoring checks are not described.

answers.justification: The same STAI and baseline/luteal schedule are described for study women in both diet groups: luteal testing at 12 days after ovum pick-up before pregnancy-test knowledge. The Discussion states all women filled the inventory within 30 minutes of the fourth luteal-support hCG injection. There is no described arm-specific instrument, threshold or extra measurement opportunity. Clinical-cycle missingness is assessed in D3; potential self-report influence from knowing the diet is assessed in 4.3-4.5.
unknowns: Individual timing adherence and questionnaire administration details by arm.

counterevidence.implication: The coping hypothesis was withheld, but diet assignment itself was apparent to participants.

answers.justification: Women themselves filled out the STAI, so they are the outcome assessors for this participant-reported state anxiety. They knew the diet they implemented after dietary instructions; blinding of a scorer or interviewer would not blind these assessors.

counterevidence.implication: Withholding the proposed coping benefit and pregnancy-test result reduces specific expectation cues, but does not make subjective self-assessment immune to diet knowledge.

answers.justification: STAI state anxiety requires subjective judgments of how a participant feels. Knowledge of following sodium restriction versus normal intake could influence those judgments or their reporting. A standardized score and withholding pregnancy-test knowledge do not eliminate this susceptibility.
unknowns: Magnitude and direction of any knowledge-related reporting influence.

counterevidence.implication: Participants necessarily knew their diet. Pilot participants had reported better coping under restriction, but their reported beliefs cannot be transferred to this trial's women as established strong expectations.

answers.justification: The investigators explicitly did not inform patients of the hypothesized role of sodium restriction in coping. With a common STAI schedule before pregnancy-test knowledge, the captured conduct gives no particular reason to judge strong diet-related expectations or reporting cues likely to distort the state-anxiety assessment. Possible influence remains, so this is not a claim of blinded or objectively measured anxiety. Actual effects of the diet on felt anxiety are part of the outcome, distinct from measurement distortion.
unknowns: Participants' individual beliefs about diet and any subtle administration cues; actual reporting influence was not measured.

bases.stopping_rationale: The Psychological tests, Diet, Introduction and Discussion sections were inspected in the sole captured report; the explicit withholding of the coping hypothesis supports a probable judgment but does not prove absence of reporting influence.
bases.unresolved_premise: Participant beliefs and direct evidence of reporting distortion remain unknown.

answers.justification: The Discussion explicitly states that a high percentage of luteal state/trait scores could not be collected because cycles were cancelled. Thus luteal state data were not available for all or nearly all randomized women. The 69 analysed compliant completers and 50 total analysis exclusions corroborate major attrition but do not define the exact observed-outcome count: some compliance exclusions may have measured scores. Baseline availability does not establish luteal availability.

exclusions: Cycle-related dropouts and no/unknown diet compliance; do not equate all exclusions with missing STAI.

scope.population: All women randomized to sodium-restricted diet in this trial

exclusions: Cycle-related dropouts and no/unknown diet compliance; do not equate all exclusions with missing STAI.

scope.population: All women randomized to normal sodium diet in this trial
scope.time_point: Luteal state anxiety assessment, 12 days after ovum pick-up

unknowns: Exact arm-specific observed luteal STAI counts and availability among compliance-excluded women.

bases.stopping_rationale: Table 1, Patient characteristics, Table 3 and the visually inspected Discussion identify substantial failed collection and analysis exclusions but do not enumerate observed outcomes separately. No additional participant-flow Source is captured.
bases.unresolved_premise: Exact luteal observation counts remain unresolved.

counterevidence.implication: The authors' claim that possible selection bias affected both diet groups similarly is relevant reassurance but rests on baseline comparisons, not evidence that luteal missingness left the selected Result unbiased.

The authors' claim that possible selection bias affected both diet groups similarly is relevant reassurance but rests on baseline comparisons, not evidence that luteal missingness left the selected Result unbiased.

answers.justification: There is no reported analysis demonstrating that the selected luteal state-anxiety result is robust to plausible outcomes in cancelled cycles. Authors rely on a non-significant diet-by-dropout interaction in baseline characteristics to claim similar possible selection bias. That baseline comparison neither recovers missing luteal scores nor tests their plausible impact on the diet contrast. The reported repeated-measurement model uses only compliant completers and supplies no missing-outcome correction or sensitivity result.
unknowns: Unreported missing-outcome analyses, if any, and outcomes among cancelled cycles.

bases.stopping_rationale: Statistical methods, Results drop-out analysis and Discussion were fully inspected; no sensitivity or missing-outcome adjustment is reported in this sole captured Source. This is not a claim that every missing-data method must be reported.
bases.unresolved_premise: No demonstrated robustness to plausible missing luteal scores is available.

counterevidence.implication: Follicle-based cancellations were protocol-defined, not documented refusals to report anxiety; this limits certainty but does not make clinical-course missingness unrelated to anxiety.

answers.justification: Missing luteal scores follow cancellation for clinical IVF-course reasons, including poor/excessive follicular response and failed fertilization. The clinical course can affect anxiety as well as whether the scheduled measurement is obtained. Dropouts already had higher mean baseline state anxiety (40.8 versus 37.8), and the authors suggest high anxiety may predispose to cancellation. These source facts make dependence of missingness on underlying luteal state anxiety plausible; this is not inferred solely from the fraction excluded.
unknowns: Actual luteal anxiety in cancelled cycles and exact overlap of clinical causes with outcome missingness.

counterevidence.implication: Authors describe selection bias as similar across arms, and the baseline state-anxiety difference is not conventionally significant. These limit certainty but do not establish independence of missing luteal values or robustness of the diet result.

Authors describe selection bias as similar across arms, and the baseline state-anxiety difference is not conventionally significant. These limit certainty but do not establish independence of missing luteal values or robustness of the diet result.

answers.justification: For state anxiety during an IVF procedure, clinical cycle failure/cancellation is likely to distinguish the emotional course from that of continuing women, and the report documents a higher baseline state-anxiety tendency among dropouts and explicitly links high state anxiety to cancellation. Combined with substantial failed luteal collection, these are reasonable grounds for probable dependence on the unobserved anxiety values, beyond a merely hypothetical measurement failure. The repeated-measurement analysis does not account for cancelled participants or their baseline anxiety to explain this relation. The p=0.11 baseline comparison is suggestive, not proof; no direction or magnitude of bias in the diet contrast is asserted.
unknowns: Whether and how strongly missingness depended on luteal state anxiety, exact arm-specific missingness proportions, and bias direction/magnitude.

bases.stopping_rationale: The relevant clinical dropout reasons, baseline dropout comparison and Discussion were inspected; missing values cannot be recovered from the captured article and no additional follow-up Source is available.
bases.unresolved_premise: Dependence is a probable clinical/source-based inference rather than a measured association with the unavailable luteal values.

answers.justification: The methods specify restricted randomization of 119 women to the two diets and cite a medical-statistics text (reference 14), rather than merely calling the trial randomized. This makes a chance-based restricted sequence probable, without establishing its generator or block details. There is no reported deterministic assignment rule.
unknowns: Sequence generator, block sizes and implementation are not described.

bases.stopping_rationale: The full main report, Randomization subsection and reference 14 were inspected. The cited reference is a general statistics textbook, not trial-specific conduct; no additional methods Source is captured.

answers.justification: The Randomization subsection identifies restricted randomization but gives no procedure preventing foreknowledge before enrolment and assignment. The captured report supplies no central service, envelopes, independent allocator or evidence of open allocation; neither probable concealment nor probable failure can reasonably be inferred for this trial.
unknowns: Concealment mechanism and recruiter access to forthcoming assignments.

bases.stopping_rationale: Inspected the complete main report and its Randomization/Setting sections; a scoped search for concealed/envelopes/allocation/sequence found no text. Source inventory contains only this article, with no trial-specific protocol or SAP.
bases.unresolved_premise: Whether forthcoming allocation was concealed is unresolved.

answers.justification: Table 2 includes all 57 restricted and 62 normal randomized women, not just completers. Age 32.3 versus 32.8, infertility duration 4.3 versus 4.0, state anxiety 40.1 versus 38.5 and trait anxiety 36.7 versus 34.0 show modest differences compatible with chance. There is no substantial excess of significant differences or marked group-size imbalance suggesting failed randomization. This does not establish concealment.
unknowns: Complete randomized-arm distribution of other prognostic factors and intended allocation ratio are not supplied.

bases.stopping_rationale: Table 2 was visually inspected with its all-randomized denominators; Patient characteristics mostly describes the 69 completers, so it is not used to infer full-arm balance.
bases.unresolved_premise: Baseline balance for prognostic factors beyond Table 2 is incompletely reported.

answers.justification: The publication describes the repeated-measurement ANOVA and least-squares means that produced the state/luteal result, but does not establish an analysis plan finalized before access to unblinded anxiety data. Ethical approval, the 1992-1995 parent-trial dates and reference to an ovarian-stimulation protocol do not establish prespecification of this anxiety analysis. No applicable plan or registry Source is captured. Reference 13 concerns renin/prorenin during stimulation, not an explicitly identified anxiety SAP; the report contains no supported public protocol/SAP URL or DOI for native acquisition.
unknowns: Pre-unblinding analysis intentions, their finalization and amendments, applicable version, and timing of investigator access to unblinded outcomes.

bases.stopping_rationale: The full article, Statistical methods, Setting and reference list were inspected, along with the Source inventory. Only the original article is captured; no explicit eligible protocol/SAP locator permits native companion acquisition. This is a bounded evidence limit, not proof that a plan never existed.
bases.unresolved_premise: Whether this Result followed pre-unblinding analysis intentions remains unknown.

counterevidence.implication: Both state and trait results at both stated occasions are reported, including nonsignificant diet tests; this weighs against demonstrated selective measurement reporting but cannot establish all original intentions.

answers.justification: State and trait STAI at baseline and luteal phase are all described and displayed in Tables 3 and 4, which is reassuring against selectively hiding these named measurements. However, no primary is designated and prospective measurement intentions are unavailable, so additional eligible scales, occasions or measurement choices cannot be established. The approved state/luteal component is a host scope choice, not evidence that trialists selected it by significance. The source does not support a yes/probably-yes claim of result-based selection, nor sufficiently complete intentions to establish absence under the official guidance.
unknowns: Complete intended eligible measurements and whether any additional measurements were collected but omitted.

bases.stopping_rationale: Psychological tests, Results and Tables 3-4 were inspected; they cover the named measures but the sole captured article supplies no prospective complete measurement plan.
bases.unresolved_premise: Completeness of eligible measurement intentions and result-based selection cannot be resolved.

counterevidence.implication: The report gives nonsignificant diet group and interaction tests alongside significant time/conception findings; this is not evidence of suppressing a known eligible diet analysis.
The report gives nonsignificant diet group and interaction tests alongside significant time/conception findings; this is not evidence of suppressing a known eligible diet analysis.

answers.justification: The selected means come from repeated-measurement ANOVA with diet, infertility, cycle number and conception. Tables distinguish group and time-by-group tests and provide baseline/luteal subclass means. Eligible alternatives could include unadjusted, baseline-adjusted or change analyses and different covariate/population choices, but the report does not say they were actually performed or chosen by their results. Without analysis intentions, it is unresolved whether this model was selected among multiple eligible analyses. The footnote mean-increase discrepancy and postrandomization conception factor are retained as analysis uncertainties, not evidence that investigators selected a favourable result.
unknowns: All intended/performed eligible analyses, model weighting/coding, and whether choices were made after examining results.

bases.stopping_rationale: Statistical methods and both anxiety results tables were inspected; no SAP, additional trial report or model-comparison history is captured. A missing plan or a mathematically unreconciled footnote does not itself establish selective analysis.
bases.unresolved_premise: Result-based selection among eligible analyses remains unresolved.

Patient characteristics
The data of 69 women who completed their cycles
with adequate compliance to the assigned diet
remained for analysis: 36 women were assigned to a
sodium restricted diet and 33 women to a n o d
sodium diet. The mean age was 332 (estimated
mean (SEM) 0.4) years. The mean duration of
infertility was 4.1 (SEM 0.4) years. Forty-three
(62%) of the women were primary infertile. Forty-
four (64%) women were enrolled in their first
IVF-ET cycle. The indications for IVF-ET were:
tubal disease (n = 23), endometriosis (n = 1 l), male
factor (n = ll), idiopathic (n = 10) and combined
factors (n = 14).
Sixty-four women were Caucasian (93%), three
were Black women and two were Asian. The
majority of the women had at least secondary
education. Fifiy-six women (81%) were employed
outdoors. Most women were employed in sales and
administrative support occupations (n = 22, 39%)
or in service occupations '(n = 16, 2%). Thirteen
women (23%) were professionals or had a high
status
Psychological tests
To assess the psychological effem, the Spielberger
State and Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI) was
usedY6J7.
These tests evaluate the level of anxiety at
a certain moment (state) and the level of anxiety
one generally feels (trait). The inventory consists of
20 items with a range of possible scores fiom 20 to
80, for state anxiety as well as for trait anxiety. The
tests were performed at baseline (just before the
time of randomization, about 10 days before the
start of the cycle) and in the luted phase of the
IVF-ET cycle (12 days after ovum pick-up), before
the patient was aware of being pregnant or not
(STM 1 and STM 2 in Figure 1). The outcome of
the pregnancy test thus could not interfere with the
STM scores. Patients were not informed about the
possible role of dietary sodium restriction on
coping skills.
Statistical methods
The moment of randomization is indicated as
baseline (before ovarian stimulation). Tmway
analysis of variance (ANOVA)
models were used to
test the effect of sodium diet and drop-out on age,
duration of infertility and the STAI scores,
respectively, for statistical significance. The
dependent variables were age, duration of infertility
and the STAI scores at baseline, respectively. The
independent variables were sodium diet (restricted,
n o d ) and dropout (yes, no). The interaction
term between sodium diet and dropout was also
included in the model. For evaluation the least-
squares means of the subclasses were assessed".
The effect of sodium diet on the STAI scores
during the cycle was analyzed using a repeated
measurement design in an ANOVA model. The
dependent variables were the state score and the
trait score, respectively. The independent variables
were sodium diet (restricted, normal), infertility
(primary, secondary), number of lVF-ET cycles
(first, repeat) and pregnancy (conception, no
conception). Here also, for evaluation the least-
squares means of the subclasses were assessed'8.

cd452baa207bc481c31ae947a5ef385127392861.transcription: A high percentage of state and trait anxiety scores in the luteal phase could not be collected because of cancellation of the IVF-ET cycle. Only a small proportion of the drop-outs were due to non-compliance with the diet. The criteria for cancellation of the cycle are laid down in the current IVF-ET protocol. Analysis of the data of the drop-outs demonstrated that possible bias by selection affected both diet groups in similar proportions. The tendency to higher mean state anxiety scores (baseline, p = 0.11) of the drop-outs compared to the scores of the women that completed their cycle suggests that high state anxiety levels may predispose to cancellation of the IVF-ET treatment. This finding confirms the effect of stress on infertility and infertility treatment as assumed by several authors before.
